one_liner: Python package with a C++17 OpenMP kernel for sparse A*B that keeps only the top-n values per row; multithreaded, so it beats single-threaded SciPy.
what_it_does: Computes the sparse product C = A.dot(B) and, optionally, keeps only the n largest entries per row (sp_matmul_topn), above an optional threshold. This is the common pattern for name matching and nearest-neighbour search over TF-IDF vectors. It is a Python API over scipy.sparse (CSR/CSC/COO in, CSR out, int32/int64/float32/float64 data), not a drop-in for A.dot(B). sp_matmul is the plain product, and zip_sp_matmul_topn merges top-n results from row-blocks of B, so a large job can be split across a cluster and stacked back together.
how_it_is_fast: The kernel is SciPy's own row-wise Gustavson SpGEMM (a modified csr_binop/csr_matmat: a dense accumulator plus a linked list of touched columns) parallelised over rows of A with OpenMP. Each thread has its own accumulator. With top-n, each row's candidates go through a fixed-size heap (std::push_heap/pop_heap, O(top_n) memory per row instead of O(n_columns)), so the full product row is never stored. In the multithreaded path each row writes into a preallocated nrows x top_n buffer, which is compacted at the end. On one thread the plain product is the same algorithm as SciPy, which is why single-thread speed is about 1.0x.
when_to_use: Top-k similarity joins (cosine similarity of L2-normalised TF-IDF or other non-negative sparse vectors) where you need only the best 10-30 matches per row: 5.5-6.9x over SciPy on 8 M2 Pro threads in the project's benchmark.
Large A x B^T products whose full result would not fit in memory, but whose top-n result does.
Multi-core machines running Python where SciPy's single-threaded sparse matmul is the bottleneck: the plain sp_matmul scales to 5.1x at 8 threads.
Matching jobs too large for one machine (O(10M+) rows): split A and B into row blocks, run each pair anywhere (the README mentions Spark), merge with zip_sp_matmul_topn and vstack.
when_not_to_use: Large top_n on few threads: top_n=1000 is 6.2x slower than SciPy on one M2 Pro thread and still 1.2x slower at 8 threads; top_n=100 on one thread is 1.9x slower.
Single-threaded use of the plain product: about 1.0x on the M2 Pro and the i9, so there is nothing to gain.
Signed data with the default threshold=None (see gotchas): from reading the source, float results at or below the smallest positive float are dropped.
General C++ SpGEMM: the headers include nanobind through common.hpp and the API exists for Python; use a C++ sparse library instead.
Very large top-n jobs on the multithreaded path: memory for the nrows x top_n buffers is allocated up front, whatever the real output size.

integration.form: module (Python package with a nanobind C++ extension; the core kernels are header-only templates under src/sparse_dot_topn_core/include)
integration.dependencies: numpy>=1.18, scipy>=1.4.1, psutil; nanobind and scikit-build-core to build; OpenMP optional (bundled in the PyPI wheels per the README; non-bundled wheels on the releases page)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 compiler for source builds; CMake 3.15+; CPython 3.9-3.14 wheels (stable-ABI cp312 wheels for 3.12+)
integration.platforms: Wheels for Windows x86-64, Linux 64-bit, macOS x86-64 and arm64. Wheels are generic builds with arch flags off; source builds add -march=native on Apple arm64 and SSE/AVX flags on x86.
integration.thread_safety: not documented (from the source: each call allocates its own buffers and the kernels keep no global state)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — sp_matmul(A, B) returns the same CSR product as A.dot(B), and sp_matmul_topn(A, B, top_n=B.shape[1]) dispatches to it, but the top-n API, parameters and defaults (unsorted output, threshold disabled) differ and B is auto-transposed when only its transpose fits

gotchas: Possible correctness bug, from reading the source and not reproduced: when threshold is None the bindings use std::numeric_limits<eT>::min() as the floor. For float/double that is the smallest positive normal (about 1.2e-38), not the lowest value, so negative and zero results never enter the top-n heap. This contradicts the README's claim that disabling threshold makes negative values work. Integer dtypes are unaffected.

Possible correctness bug, from reading the source and not reproduced: plain sp_matmul sizes C_indptr with a symbolic pass that counts every touched column, but the numeric pass skips sums that are exactly 0. If values cancel, or the input stores explicit zeros, the single-thread path shifts later rows' entries against indptr and the multithreaded path leaves unwritten slots, so the output holds uninitialised memory. The tests use only non-negative sparse.random data.

The multithreaded top-n path computes nrows*top_n and per-row offsets in the index type (int32 when indices fit) and sums row counts with an int accumulator. Very large nrows x top_n (above 2^31) can overflow.
n_threads=None means one thread, and -1 means physical cores minus one. Without OpenMP the call warns and runs single-threaded. COO and CSC inputs are converted to CSR first, which costs time.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Of the catalogued siblings, only VBCSR also targets SciPy sparse. Pick sparse_dot_topn for unstructured TF-IDF-style similarity search with a small top-n, and VBCSR for block-structured operators. For general multithreaded SpGEMM inside C++ code, TACO-generated kernels or ALP/GraphBLAS fit better, because this package's kernels are tied to its Python bindings.
verified_claims_summary: The project's richbench run (30 repeats, SciPy 1.12.0 vs sparse-dot-topn v1.0.0, two 20,000 x 193,190 TF-IDF matrices of SEC EDGAR company names) shows the plain product 5.1x faster on 8 threads of an Apple M2 Pro (0.032 s vs 0.165 s) and 3.4x on an 8-core 2.3 GHz Intel i9. top_n=10 reaches 6.9x (M2 Pro) and 12.7x (i9) at 8 threads. Single-thread plain product is about 1.0x, and top_n>=100 on one thread is slower than SciPy. The compiler and flags of the benchmarked build are not stated.
status_note: Active (v1.2.0 adds CPython 3.14 wheels; last commit 2026-09-14), Apache-2.0, 425 stars and 3 open issues. Easy to pip install, but the kernels are coupled to nanobind, so vendoring them into a C++ project takes some unpicking.
